questions.prompt: What makes a finished project useful as a portfolio piece?
choices: Someone else can find it, work out what it does, and run it
It has no bugs left in it
questions.explain: A reader who cannot run it has only your word for what it does. That is why the README and a tidy repository count for as much as the code.

questions.prompt: Which of these are reasonable next steps after a first project?
choices: Add one of the nice-to-haves you scoped out
Rewrite the parts you now know a better way to write
Start a second project that uses something new
Wait until you know enough before building again
questions.explain: All three of those keep you writing code. Waiting until you know enough is the one that stops, and nobody ever reaches that point anyway.

questions.prompt: You finished the project, but you had to look things up constantly. What does that tell you?
choices: You did not really learn the material
Not much on its own, since looking things up is how the work is done, including professionally
You should start again without help
The project was above your level
questions.explain: What you can look up is not what was being tested. Knowing what to search for, and recognising the right answer when you find it, is the part that got better.

questions.prompt: Match each thing you built to the skill it is evidence of.
left: A README somebody else managed to follow
Cutting three features to finish on time
right: Handling a failure the user will actually hit
Writing for a reader who is not you
Organising code so it stays workable
questions.explain: Every one of these is a decision rather than a piece of syntax, and decisions are what a project shows that an exercise cannot.
